Portfolio Construction & Position Management

The Operating System

Three behaviors, one portfolio.

Part 5 is where the framework stops describing and starts building: which positions to hold, how large, in which accounts, and under what rules they stay or go. Part 6 supplies the two scores all of it depends on.

Start with a distinction the industry blurs. Asset selection answers what to own. Portfolio construction answers how each position should behave inside the whole, and that behavior is what the framework classifies. Every position except Bitcoin carries exactly one of three behavioral .

Posture 01 Torque Controlled convexity

Deliberate leverage on regime forces that are real, durable, and capital-backed, yet still early, underowned, or mis-sized by institutions. Torque carries the upside and absorbs the drawdowns.

2–15%per position 40–60%aggregate Posture 02 Ballast Strategic reserve

Capital built to survive what breaks everything else: liquidity stress, policy error, narrative reversal. Ballast holds steady while Torque swings, then buys the dislocation.

1–8%per position 20–35%aggregate Posture 03 Hype Disciplined speculation

Narrative momentum with no capital commitment underneath: useful as a trade, unsafe as a foundation. Hype lives under hard caps and an exit committed to before entry, and it is never allowed to carry load.

2–5%per position ≤10%hard cap

These aggregate ranges are doctrine; the dashboard does not build to them, and it measures posture drift against the targets your operating thesis implies (Part 6).

Why three? Because removing any one breaks the portfolio in a predictable way. Strip out and every drawdown hands you a forced choice: sell at trough prices, or hold it with no dry powder. Strip out Torque and the portfolio keeps its capital and stops compounding: safe, and going nowhere. Let in without governance and reflexive narrative positions grow until one of them breaks the book.

Bitcoin sits outside all three. It is the convexity backbone from Part 3, scored like every other holding, but the score does not size, gate or sell it. Part 3’s rules govern it: accumulate only, pace set by valuation discipline, held outside the three postures and the concentration limits. Nothing in this part sells it or draws on it to fund anything else, though Ballast income may fund its purchases during a dislocation. The exhibit below runs all four through one market cycle.

Read the postures as jobs. Torque’s job, turning a thesis into convex exposure, comes first, because the rest of the structure exists to carry it.

Controlled Convexity

Torque: leverage on regime forces.

Torque 2–15%per position 40–60%aggregate · high conviction 50–70%drawdown tolerance

Torque is where the framework takes its risk on purpose: a bet on a structural shift you believe is real, durable and capital-backed, which institutions are underexposed to because mandates, compliance processes or volatility limits keep them out. Returns are lopsided by design: a minority of positions deliver the multi-baggers while the rest underperform. And Torque can fall 50 to 70 percent during liquidity stress. That is the price of convexity; position sizing and Ballast exist to make it payable.

Entry is earned three ways at once. Miss any one and the position does not qualify.

  1. Structural tailwind from identifiable regime forces. The position must benefit directly from durable macro forces; general market beta or sector rotation does not count. Part 2 sets out how to build a regime thesis, and the forces themselves vary by practitioner. Examples: Fourth Turning demographic stress, AI infrastructure buildout, defense modernization, energy constraint, monetary disorder.

  2. Business model survivability under stress. Funding secured, customer concentration manageable, and a balance sheet that can ride out a 12–24 month liquidity drought. Many small-caps with exceptional TAM headroom still fail here, because they need the capital markets open to survive; the ones that qualify have reached profitability, secured non-dilutive funding, or hold cash runways longer than any plausible stress period.

  3. Valuation headroom sufficient for convex payoff. The addressable market should be much larger than the current market cap, often 5× or more. A $500 billion company would have to become a $10 trillion company to return 20×. Torque therefore skews toward small and mid-caps, where the headroom exists, though market cap alone neither qualifies nor disqualifies.

Passing the gate earns a position its place, not its size. Size is earned in stages, as evidence accumulates: the ladder below records what has been proven and carries no percentages by design. The percentages come from the score, through the band table that follows.

The is the composite score Part 6 builds from four components: convexity, risk, macro alignment, and execution. The posture picks the table and the score picks the band within it, and because the bands are set in advance, no threshold has to be argued twice. Read each band as a ceiling: its top is the most a score in it can justify, and its lower bound is not a floor. The dashboard’s portfolio builder scales that ceiling with the score and lowers it when data confidence is low: at full confidence a Torque 70 justifies at most 8 percent and an 85 about 11.5 percent (formula on the Math page).

Torque sizing bands: CIS score to allocation band
CIS score Allocation band Sizing rationale
70+8–15%Core Torque position. Full conviction sizing, subject to the concentration limits below
60–694–8%Standard Torque position. Allocation-worthy but constrained until conviction strengthens across components
50–592–4%Starter position. Thesis incomplete or fragile; size reflects probe intent, not commitment
<500%Not allocation-worthy. Avoid, trim, or reclassify; no posture sizes a score below 50, so reclassifying does not restore eligibility

Concentration limits apply irrespective of CIS: single position 15% default cap · 18% absolute maximum with documented override · top three ≤35% combined · top five ≤50% · Bitcoin operates under separate rules · the dashboard flags a breach on the book you hold; it does not block the trade · scores in the 50s and 60s are permitted, but the FIS (Part 6) charges each a small, value-weighted governance penalty

Where Torque lives.

Account routing follows expected turnover: the more often a position is likely to be sold, the stronger the case for Roth. The account rules come from Part 4; the table applies them to Torque.

Torque wrapper routing by expected turnover
Wrapper Torque it suits Why
Roth IRATorque expected to rotateRotation compounds tax-free regardless of holding period
TaxableBuy-and-hold beyond one year; Roth overflowLong-term capital gains treatment; harvesting pairs available
Pre-taxTactical onlyViable during accumulation with decades until withdrawal, when the current marginal rate exceeds the expected retirement rate, and when bracket arbitrage or a later Roth conversion is actually planned

Taxable also favors liquidity, loss harvesting, and return-of-capital income · Bitcoin is exempt from this routing and sits in taxable cold storage by default (Part 3)

Torque Governance

  • Earnings proximity. A position is capped at 3% of the portfolio from T-5, five trading days before its earnings report, through the report. Proceeds park in cash or Ballast inside the same account until the rebuild. The cap is non-negotiable; its 3% level is a calibration parameter (Protocol 01, below).
  • Momentum tripwires. Exit when all three momentum dimensions turn negative, even if CIS remains high; re-entry is permitted once momentum repairs (Protocol 02, below).
  • Drawdown tolerance. Hold through large drawdowns when Ballast reserves are adequate and momentum dimensions remain mixed or positive, subject to the −20 percent freeze: a position 20 percent or more below cost takes no new capital without a confirming signal (Protocol 04, below). Selling Torque at trough prices on price alone, while momentum is still mixed and the thesis holds, is a framework failure. The one exit price can call on its own is the momentum tripwire above, when all three dimensions turn negative; a broken core assertion (Protocol 05) or a thesis damaged by earnings (Protocol 01) is an exit whatever the price.
  • Review cadence. Weekly CIS review, monthly formal reassessment. Material news triggers an immediate review.

Strategic Reserves

Ballast: the reserve that buys the drawdown.

Ballast 1–8%per position 20–35%aggregate · working range 15%floor · 40% ceiling

Torque that can fall 50 to 70 percent is holdable only if part of the portfolio refuses to fall with it. That is Ballast’s job, and the reason aggressive Torque sizing is possible at all. Ballast businesses fund their dividends when credit tightens and keep operating without access to capital markets.

What earns Ballast its space is rotation. After Torque runs, trim any position that has grown past its concentration limit or past the size its score justifies, and move the proceeds into Ballast; deploy Ballast into Torque during drawdowns that momentum and the thesis still support, and into a position 20 percent or more below cost only after the confirming signal the freeze requires. That loop is the framework’s primary way of buying low without raising outside cash or selling Bitcoin.

Five tests, three required.

A position qualifies by passing at least three of the five tests below. Yield is deliberately not one of them: income can follow from qualifying, but it never qualifies a position on its own.

  1. Fortress balance sheet

    Net cash or minimal leverage, no near-term refinancing, investment-grade or equivalent strength.

  2. Diversified revenue

    No single customer exceeds 15% of revenue, geographic diversification, no dependence on a single product cycle.

  3. Durable cash generation

    Consistent free cash flow through cycles, dividend history, capital allocation discipline.

  4. Low factor correlation

    Limited sensitivity to equity beta, real rates, and credit spreads. Moves independently of Torque during stress.

  5. Liquidity-resilient valuation

    Reasonable multiples with downside limited by a valuation floor, not a growth narrative.

Sizing and placement.

Ballast scores lower than Torque of equivalent quality, by construction. The Convexity component carries 30 to 45 percent of the CIS composite depending on the thesis profile (40 percent at the reference weights), and capital-preserving positions lack the TAM headroom behind high Convexity sub-scores. The same four bands apply, with smaller ranges scaled to a reserve’s job.

Ballast sizing bands: CIS score to allocation band
CIS score Allocation band Sizing rationale
70+5–8%Core Ballast position. Survivability and macro alignment strong enough to overcome the structural Convexity headwind
60–693–5%Standard Ballast position. Capital preservation and rotation utility within the portfolio
50–591–3%Marginal Ballast. Must meet eligibility criteria (3 of 5) and demonstrate improving quality or face replacement
<500%Not Ballast-worthy. Exit or replace

One position may reach 10% for exceptional stability · aggregate Ballast: 20–35% working range, 15% floor at all times, 40% ceiling

One concrete reference point is STRC, Strategy Inc.’s variable-rate perpetual preferred stock and the income instrument the framework names as Ballast. STRC qualifies as Ballast under the three-of-five rule on durable cash generation (for a preferred, its distribution record: paid in every period since issuance), low factor correlation (the monthly rate reset is designed to hold its price near its $100 stated amount) and a liquidity-resilient valuation (its $100 stated amount and rate-reset support). It carries no agency credit rating as a new instrument; the framework reads the issuer’s Bitcoin asset coverage as its measure of balance-sheet strength. The issuer resets the rate monthly; it was 12 percent a year, paid semi-monthly, as of September 2026, and your yield depends on the price you paid. Bitcoin drawdowns can compress the issuer’s distributable income and STRC’s market price. Return-of-capital characterization is set each tax year and verified on Form 1099-DIV. The case study at the end of this part notes its 2026 price history, and Part 4 covers how its distributions are taxed.

Placement follows the distribution profile. Taxable is the main home, especially for return-of-capital income and for tax-loss harvesting. Pre-tax suits ordinary-income payers, such as bond funds and REITs whose distributions are not return of capital, where pre-tax space exists. Roth is usually wasted on Ballast, because Roth pays most on the positions that grow the most.

Ballast Governance

  • Rotation triggers. Trim Torque that has run past its concentration limit or the size its score justifies into Ballast; deploy Ballast into Torque drawdowns when momentum remains constructive, subject to the −20 percent freeze.
  • Yield deployment. Distributions accumulate as deployment capital. During stress or Bitcoin dislocations, yield funds without selling depressed positions.
  • Minimum reserve. Aggregate Ballast stays at or above 15 percent at all times; deployment spends only what sits above the floor, and the post-run trim rebuilds the reserve toward its working range.
  • Quality threshold. Positions must keep meeting the eligibility criteria (3 of 5). A stronger candidate replaces a weaker holding instead of adding to the count.
  • Review cadence. Its CIS is reviewed in the weekly pass like every position’s; the formal Ballast reassessment is quarterly, sooner on material deterioration.
  • Named exception. STRC currently occupies the 12 percent income and deployment slot under a documented exception to the ordinary 10 percent single-Ballast maximum, reviewed at each quarterly Ballast reassessment and sooner on material deterioration. It keeps the slot while it meets three of the five eligibility criteria and no stronger candidate appears. At each quarterly reassessment, compare STRC with every cash-distributing Ballast candidate in the dashboard’s current discovery universe that meets at least three eligibility criteria. A candidate is stronger if it meets more of the five criteria than STRC, or meets as many and has a CIS at least 5 points higher at two consecutive reassessments. The Evidence page logs the full set and result, including “no eligible alternative”.

Disciplined Speculation

Hype: quarantined, capped, and pre-committed to exit.

Hype 2–5%per position ≤10%aggregate · hard cap 15–25%stop-loss below entry

Torque and Ballast govern the capital the portfolio depends on. Hype governs the capital it can afford to lose, chasing asymmetric short-term payoffs where markets misprice assets on sentiment extremes, regulatory shifts or technical dislocations, with nothing structural underneath. Its prices run on attention and reflexive feedback, and they have no floor when the narrative breaks. A Torque position that falls 50 percent can recover, because the regime forces persist. A Hype position that falls 80 percent may be gone for good, and the portfolio never needed it. Many portfolios hold no Hype at all, and are right to.

The catastrophic failure mode is not holding Hype. It is holding Hype while calling it Torque.

Whatever its label says, a position is Hype when it shows any of these signs.

Price-attention reflexivity

Price gains drive attention, which drives buying, which drives price, with no business momentum underneath. The loop can generate 500% in months and give back 90% in weeks. If you cannot point to a lasting improvement in the business, it’s Hype.

Valuation disconnected from plausible scenarios

A $500 million company with $10 million of revenue at 50× sales requires assumptions that strain credibility. It can still pay as Hype. It should not be held as Torque.

Funding-dependent survival

Pre-revenue companies burning cash with no route to profitability. When the capital markets tighten, they run out of road.

Visible but unpriced moat erosion

The competitive advantage is degrading and the price has not caught up. It can work as Hype until the narrative breaks, never as Torque: there is no recovery once reality arrives.

Hype Governance

  • Momentum is the thesis and the exit signal. Enter only on technical breakouts with volume confirmation. Buy strength.
  • Stop-loss protocol. Exit at 15–25% below entry, set when you buy. No widening stops, no averaging down, no converting to “long-term hold.” Exit and reassess.
  • Sizing and cap. Eligible from CIS 50; 2–5% per position; no Hype position exceeds 5% under any circumstances, and no override exists; 10% strict aggregate cap.
  • Profit-taking ladder. One-third off at a 50% gain, another third at 100%, remainder runs with the stop raised to breakeven.
  • Time limit. Exit positions that have not worked within 3–6 months rather than waiting for the stop-loss.
  • Reclassification prohibition. Hype cannot be reclassified to Torque to justify holding through a stop-loss breach.

Of these rules, the dashboard’s portfolio builder applies the caps, sizing Hype from CIS50 at no more than 5 percent a position and 10 percent in aggregate. On the portfolio you hold, it flags a breach of either cap for review, and its Stop Loss tripwire flags a Hype position 25 percent or more below cost; it records every trade and places no stops. The 15 to 25 percent stops and the 3 to 6 month time limits are yours.

The exhibit below sets the three postures side by side. A CIS score measures quality; the job a position does decides how much capital that quality earns. A CIS70 in Torque sits in the 8 to 15 percent band, and the same CIS70 in Ballast in the 5 to 8 percent band: both strong, at different things.

The portfolio-wide single-position cap, 15 percent by default and 18 percent absolute with a documented override, applies to every posture, but by default only Torque can reach it: Ballast stops at 10 percent unless a documented override holds a position higher (the case study below has one), and Hype stops at 5, with no override. Posture decides what a score is worth, the concentration limits decide how much any one name may matter, and the protocols in the next section keep it that way.

Position Management

Governance through the cycle.

Construction is a moment; management is the practice that follows. Six protocols keep the structure true through the cycle: earnings exposure, momentum, regime stress, additions, thesis integrity, and known events beyond earnings. Each says which part the dashboard watches and which part is yours.

Protocol 01 · The 3% cap is flagged live; the trim is yours

Earnings proximity: cap the binary event.

Earnings are binary events. A company can beat estimates and fall because expectations ran higher; it can miss and rally because the miss was smaller than feared. A single report can move a position 10 to 30 percent either way, especially the smaller growth names Torque favors, and conviction about business quality predicts none of it. So the framework sizes around earnings instead of forecasting them.

A position entering its final five trading days before earnings may not exceed 3 percent of portfolio value. The trim happens in one step at T-5, and the cap holds through the report. Take a defense contractor at 10 percent of the portfolio: five trading days before its report it is trimmed to 3 percent, and the proceeds park in cash or Ballast inside the same account until the rebuild. If the thesis is confirmed, the rebuild starts at T+6. Under the weekly add cap of a quarter of the target (Protocol 04), a rebuild takes two to four weeks for positions sized between about 5 and 15 percent (three weeks for a 10 percent position: 5.5, 8, then 10 percent).

Earnings proximity protocol by trading-day window
Timeframe Rule Rationale
T-21 to T-6Initiation blackout for positions priced for perfectionAvoid entering at maximum expectation levels
T-5 to T-1Cap the position entering earnings at 3% of portfolioLimit binary event exposure for that specific name
T+0No action; observe the reactionLet the market process information
T+1 to T+5Assessment windowEvaluate thesis impact from results and the call
T+6 onwardsRebuild eligible if thesis confirmedGradually restore position sizing

Post-earnings decision tree: thesis confirmed → rebuild over 2–4 weeks · thesis damaged → complete exit irrespective of loss, no averaging down · thesis uncertain → hold reduced until clarity emerges

The dashboard flags a position above the 3 percent cap in the days before its report. It counts calendar days, not trading days, so the flag can arrive a trading day or two after T-5; start the trim from the earnings calendar instead of waiting for the flag. It trims nothing: the trim is yours, and so is the T-21 to T-6 initiation blackout. Three exemptions apply by doctrine, though the dashboard flags any position above the cap that has a report date on file, exempt or not. Bitcoin has no earnings and answers to Part 3. Broad index ETFs diversify away single-name earnings risk. And Ballast positions at or below 5 percent, where earnings are not thesis-critical, are left alone: a single report rarely threatens a stable name’s classification, so the burden exceeds the benefit.

Protocol 02 · Doctrine · not yet measured live

Momentum: conviction requires confirmation.

The framework asks the market to confirm what you believe, along three dimensions. Absolute momentum is distance from the 52-week high: within 10 percent is healthy, 25 percent or more below is a correction, and 40 percent or more below is severe distress. Relative momentum is performance against the sector and the market, which tells you whether the problem is the company or the tape. Breadth is the share of related names making new highs: broad participation confirms fundamental support, and narrowing leadership warns of exhaustion. How many of the three break decides how much capital a thesis may carry; which one breaks does not matter.

The momentum action ladder: dimensions broken to required action
Dimensions negative Action Register
NoneFull sizing per the CIS bandStandard
OneReduce sizing 25–30%; monitor closelyCaution
TwoWatch status; minimal new exposureRestricted
All threeExit, even if the CIS score is still highTripwire

The last rung is a tripwire · exit, reassess, and re-enter when the momentum filter repairs

The exit rung is the framework’s hardest discipline, because the fires on what the market is doing while your conviction is still saying hold. The same that forced the exit decides when you may come back.

The dashboard does not yet measure these three dimensions. Its Momentum Death tripwire reports unavailable rather than guessing, and a moving-average and RSI screen is coded but not yet fed any price data. What it does watch is stress across your holdings as a group: a cohort confluence tripwire that escalates as more warning signs coincide, from a flag, to hedging only, to a displayed playbook for trimming the Torque cohort by 25 percent. Running that playbook is yours. The Math page lists the ten signals and how they escalate.

Three companion heuristics, borrowed loosely from Newton’s laws of motion, shape the day-to-day.

  1. Inertia

    Positions in motion deserve patience. A position flat for 90 days deserves a fresh look at its thesis.

  2. Proportionality

    Larger positions need larger catalysts. A 12 percent Torque position trims on material fundamental change; a 3 percent probe can exit on technical deterioration alone.

  3. Consequences

    Allocation is zero-sum. Before any action, name where the proceeds go and which position is implicitly underweighted.

Momentum Overrides Conviction

A position can be fundamentally right and still destroy capital through extended technical deterioration. Exiting keeps the capital and the option to re-enter; it concedes only that the market is not validating the thesis yet.

Protocol 03 · Correlation above 0.70 is flagged live

Liquidity and correlation: throttle the regime.

Sometimes the problem is not the position but the water it swims in. When cross-asset correlation rises and liquidity drains away, positions that looked independent in calm markets trade as one, and Torque drawdowns outgrow any single-name analysis. The response is a throttle, run as a state machine rather than a judgment call.

The stressed-regime indicators are VIX sustained above 25, credit spreads widening, and Torque positions correlating above 0.7. The dashboard watches all three as signals: its macro tripwires track the VIX and high-yield credit spreads, and its Correlation Spike tripwire fires when the average pairwise correlation of all your non-cash holdings, not Torque alone, rises above 0.70, reporting unavailable rather than calm when price history is too short (the Math page has the thresholds). When a tripwire breaches, the Add Position screen recommends pausing additions and still records the trade. The response is yours, and deliberately boring: pause new Torque adds, hold posture limits strictly, consider reducing gross exposure 10 to 20 percent, and return to standard positioning only after stress indicators normalize for two weeks or more. None of this is market timing: it cuts exposure only when correlation makes position-level diversification unreliable.

Protocol 04 · Doctrine · pacing is yours

Adds and freezes: discipline on the way in.

Averaging down without rules is how conviction destroys portfolios, so additions are governed too. A position 20 percent or more below its cost basis is frozen: no new capital without a confirming signal, such as a higher low, a reclaimed key level, or new information that supports the thesis. Scaling in happens over weeks, never more than a quarter of the target in one week. Frequency limits pace the rest: a position’s score is recalculated at most every 7 days (except after material news), adds come at least 3 days apart (except in an earnings rebuild), partial trims at least 5 days apart (except under earnings proximity), and an exit is never rate-limited when a tripwire fires.

Pacing works like the concentration caps: the −20 percent freeze and the weekly add cap are practitioner discipline, and the dashboard records every trade you make and never blocks one. Its Weekly Review paces only its own advice: it waits 5 days before repeating a resize recommendation for the same position, never delays an earnings-window trim or a tripwire response, and leaves a score younger than 7 days alone. Nothing in the dashboard spaces your adds, so the 3-day interval is yours too.

Protocol 05 · One to three core assertions per position

Thesis drift: price problems versus truth problems.

Every position carries one to three core assertions written down at entry: “defense budget growth sustains through 2027,” “datacenter capex has three or more years to run,” “management is executing on margin expansion.” When a core assertion breaks, reassessment is immediate and price is irrelevant: the position is downgraded or exited, and a later price recovery does not rehabilitate a broken thesis. Momentum rules handle the price problem; this protocol handles the truth problem.

Protocol 06 · Earnings-style treatment

Known events beyond earnings.

Regulatory decisions, policy announcements, contract awards and insider lockup expirations all get earnings-style treatment: keep a calendar of known binary events for each position and apply the earnings protocol to each, capping the position ahead of the event or hedging it. Diffuse macro noise, such as Fed meetings and election cycles, triggers nothing unless it bears directly on a thesis. Every protocol in this section governs positions one at a time; the next section widens the lens to the forces those positions share.

Regime Forces

Allocate by force, not by sector.

The unit of allocation is the force. A sector matters only to the extent it captures a structural force the practitioner has identified (Part 2 sets out how), and the five forces named in Torque’s entry test serve as the examples.

Mapping one example thesis.

Under the example thesis, the regime-aligned sectors are concrete: defense and aerospace (government customers, multi-year visibility, pricing power, strong balance sheets); AI infrastructure (semiconductors, datacenter buildout and power delivery, favoring picks-and-shovels businesses with order backlogs over speculative plays); energy infrastructure (traditional and nuclear power, grid modernization); and industrials tied to reshoring, chosen selectively, because many industrials are cyclical with no structural tailwind.

The same thesis names the regime-challenged sectors it avoids: long-duration unprofitable growth that depends on low rates (Hype if at all, never Torque), consumer discretionary without pricing power, and commercial real estate facing secular office decline and a refinancing wall.

Concentration in a force is intentional; concentration in a sector is not. The method is to diversify within the force: own several economically distinct businesses that earn from the same driver through different mechanisms, so one sector’s failure cannot take the thesis down with it. The example illustrates the method; it does not recommend the sectors shown.

A practitioner bullish on AI infrastructure expresses it through semiconductors, datacenter REITs, power infrastructure and cooling technology, rather than through 45 percent in one sector. The limits below hold that shape in place.

Sector allocation limits under regime concentration
Constraint Limit Rationale
Any single sector (ex-Bitcoin)30% maximumLimits idiosyncratic sector risk
Top 2 sectors combined50% maximumEnsures minimum diversification
Regime-challenged sectors10% maximumTactical only, never core

Bitcoin is excluded from sector limits: it is the convexity backbone, governed separately (Part 3)

High-conviction Torque regimes require diversification across multiple expressions of the same regime force, not single-sector concentration.

Conviction and Friction

Rebalancing as conviction expression.

Force-level allocation sets the portfolio’s shape; rebalancing decides when the shape may change. The framework rejects mechanical rebalancing, on a calendar or back to fixed percentage bands. Drift past a threshold triggers a review, and the review decides; nothing trades on its own. Mechanical rules ignore what the price move is saying. A position up 50 percent may have appreciated for a reason, and trimming it on a schedule sells winners for winning. A position down 30 percent may be breaking, and adding to it on a schedule catches a falling knife.

So rebalancing follows conviction. On upward drift, recalculate CIS: if conviction is unchanged, let it run; if it has declined, trim. On downward drift, recalculate CIS: if conviction is intact and the decline temporary, add, after the confirming signal Protocol 04 requires once a position is 20 percent or more below cost; if conviction has declined, reduce or exit. Between weekly passes, a rebalancing review is called for when a position moves 15 percent or more in a single week, when the earnings protocol triggers, when a tripwire breaches, or when material news changes the thesis. Part 6 sets out the weekly routine and the two other events that call for an early look: a single-day move of more than 5 percent (the dashboard lists any move of 5 percent or more on its Governance page) and a CIS update from new research.

The tax dimension.

Every rebalancing decision also has a tax side. Part 4 shows why the account a position sits in can matter as much as the position; turnover is where that advantage is kept or given away. Run the arithmetic once. Take $100,000 earning 10 percent a year before tax for 30 years, with each year’s gains realized and taxed at a 25 percent blended rate: the same asset, traded the same way, in two different accounts. Taxed every year, it compounds at 7.5 percent. In a Roth, the full 10 percent survives.

The terminal values are about $875,000 in the account taxed every year and about $1,745,000 in the Roth: a gap of roughly $870,000, so the Roth ends with about twice the wealth from placement alone. The 25 percent rate is illustrative, and the Roth figure assumes qualified withdrawals under current law. Part 4’s Tax Wedge works the case of a gain realized once; this exhibit works gains realized every year, compounding through time.

In Roth, rebalance without friction; that freedom is why rotating Torque lives there, not a reason to rotate. In taxable, prefer new contributions over selling; when a sale is necessary, sell long-term holdings first and coordinate with tax-loss harvesting. Across accounts, treat every rebalancing event as a chance to re-check placement: a position whose expected turnover has changed may belong in a different account, which usually means steering new money there, since cash taken out of a Roth or pre-tax account is a distribution. Every rule in this part holds only if changes to the rules are themselves governed, and that is the last section’s job.

Change Governance

Doctrine, parameters, overrides.

Every framework decays the same way: one small unexamined change at a time. A threshold is nudged, a stop widened, a cap waived just this once, until the framework is a memory wearing its own name. The defense is to classify every change before making it: a doctrine change means abandoning the framework, a parameter change means calibration, and an override means a temporary, documented deviation for stated reasons.

What Lives At Each Level

  • Doctrine: non-negotiable principles. These define what the framework is; break one and you are no longer running ACF. Three-posture classification for every position except Bitcoin · account placement treated as a first-order return decision · Bitcoin as the non-negotiable convexity backbone, always held, its size and accumulation pace governed by Part 3 · all three momentum dimensions turning negative triggers an exit regardless of conviction · Hype positions require stop-losses and cannot be reclassified to avoid them · Ballast eligibility requires meeting hard criteria, not approximations.
  • Parameters: tunable thresholds. Adjustable for valid, stated reasons while preserving the framework’s integrity. CIS component weights (reference C 40% · R 25% · M 25% · E 10%; each thesis profile moves them within 0.10) · position sizing bands within postures (e.g. 2–15% for Torque) · momentum dimension thresholds (10%/25%/40% from the 52-week high) · earnings proximity cap level (default 3%; the cap itself is doctrine, its level is calibration) · concentration limits (default 15% single position, raised only by documented override and never past the 18% absolute maximum; 35% top three, 50% top five) · Ballast aggregate ceiling (default 40%).
  • Overrides: explicit user decisions. Conscious deviations from default parameters. Each is intentional, documented and time-bounded, states its reasoning and the conditions for reversion, and stays consistent with the framework’s objectives. The framework remains the baseline; overrides are exceptions, not evolution.

Silent drift is not an override. A stop “temporarily” widened without a note is the signature of a framework being abandoned while its owner still believes in it. Overrides exist so that deviation stays visible, reasoned and reversible.

The portfolio boundary and single-name sleeves.

The portfolio boundary is the household aggregate across all accounts: Roth, pre-tax, taxable and Bitcoin cold storage. Every concentration limit (single position, top three, top five, sector) applies to that aggregate, not to individual accounts, and a position held in several accounts counts as one exposure. An account may therefore be concentrated when the household is not: a Roth IRA can hold 100 percent of its value in one position, provided the household’s exposure stays inside the caps. An account concentrated in one name on purpose is designated a single-name sleeve, in writing; its drift is monitored, and it is trimmed or rebalanced if aggregate exposure breaches a limit. A sleeve is a way of governing concentration, never a way around the limits.

The case study below puts this part’s rules to work in one illustrative portfolio.

Torque45%Ballast30%Hype5%Bitcoin20%

Case Study: Three-Posture Construction (Illustrative)

One practitioner’s implementation of a specific regime thesis; a different thesis would produce different sector allocations under the same method. Context: a $500,000 portfolio, high conviction in an AI-infrastructure and defense-modernization thesis, moderate risk tolerance, 15-year horizon. The scores are illustrative, not dashboard output. Sizes here are a practitioner’s placements within each band. For five of them (the AI semiconductor leader, the defense prime contractor, the dividend growth ETF, defensive healthcare and the momentum breakout play), the dashboard’s portfolio builder would set a lower, score-scaled ceiling; STRC is held under an override (below).

  • Bitcoin backbone (20% · $100,000). Cold storage per Part 3, outside the three postures. Taxable account, held to pass to heirs with a stepped-up basis under current law; borrowing against it stays an optional later phase under Part 3’s rules, once the reserve has grown into the mature share. Twenty percent is the low end of Part 3’s 20–30 percent elevated range, which Part 3 ties to higher conviction and longer horizons; this case takes it for its 15-year horizon.
  • Torque (45% · $225,000 across 8 positions). AI semiconductor leader 10% (CIS 75, thesis confirmed, near 52-week high; Roth) · defense prime contractor 9% (CIS 72, multi-year backlog; Roth) · nuclear renaissance play 7% (CIS 70, uranium supply/demand inflection; taxable, long-term hold) · AI datacenter REIT 5% (CIS 67, hyperscaler expansion; taxable, though its distributions are mostly ordinary income, which pre-tax space would shelter better) · defense mid-cap specialist 5% (CIS 65, scaling; Roth) · grid infrastructure 4% (CIS 62, electrification tailwind; taxable) · small-cap AI picks-and-shovels 3% (CIS 57, early thesis development; Roth) · reshoring beneficiary 2% (CIS 53, monitoring for confirmation; taxable).
  • Ballast (30% · $150,000: three positions plus the liquidity sleeve). STRC 12% (CIS 71; yielding about 11 percent as of January 2026, with return-of-capital treatment verified each year on Form 1099-DIV; taxable, provides deployment capital) · dividend growth ETF 8% (CIS 70, broad quality exposure; taxable) · liquidity parking sleeve 6% (no CIS: a cash-equivalent reserve for rebalancing and for trim proceeds raised in taxable; not structural Ballast) · defensive healthcare 4% (CIS 62, non-cyclical stability; pre-tax, filling existing 401(k) space). At 12 percent, STRC sits above the 10 percent single-Ballast maximum and the 5 to 8 percent band its score earns. The case holds it there under a documented override: it is the book’s return-of-capital income and deployment sleeve, and the override is reviewed at each quarterly Ballast reassessment. STRC’s weight and yield are those of the case as built in January 2026. Update, September 2026. On June 26, 2026, during a Bitcoin selloff, STRC closed at $74.57 (intraday low $71.25); it was back above $84 by June 30 and closed at $99.56 on September 29, close to its 52-week high of $100.42. Distributions were paid throughout; the rate is 12 percent a year, paid semi-monthly.
  • Hype (5% · $25,000 across 2 positions). Momentum breakout play 3% (CIS 54, 20% stop-loss; taxable, short-term expected, so a stop-out leaves a harvestable loss and a win is taxed as a short-term gain) · speculative small-cap 2% (CIS 51, 25% stop-loss; taxable, for the same reason).
  • Aggregate. A weighted average CIS of about 68 across the scored positions. Roth holds the Torque most likely to rotate; taxable holds Bitcoin, the stable Ballast and the long-duration holds; pre-tax is minimal. Earnings proximity in action: the defense prime contractor enters its T-5 window, so the 9% position ($45,000) is trimmed to 3% ($15,000), with the $30,000 held as cash inside the Roth, counted toward the liquidity sleeve at household level, until the post-earnings rebuild.

Scope

The sizing bands, thresholds and examples in this part are framework defaults and illustrations, not recommendations for any specific investor. Descriptions of what the dashboard does are as of September 2026. This framework does not constitute investment, tax, or legal advice. Consult qualified professionals for your specific situation.

End of Part 5

Part 5 sorted every position except Bitcoin into one of three postures, sized and placed each one, and set the protocols that keep the structure honest through the cycle. The posture logic carries to other markets by substituting local proxies for the regime forces; the account rules do not, because they follow United States tax law.
